common_name: Younique Carmine Astilbe (Compact Early-Blooming Heavy Shade Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Younique Carmine is a Dutch-bred selection noted for tolerating deeper shade and blooming earlier than most astilbe cultivars.

directions: Set crowns so the top of the rhizome sits just below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade. Younique Carmine forms a tidy mound of glossy, dark green, fern-textured foliage topped by dense, upright plumes of carmine-red flowers that open in succession from early to midsummer, giving a long display compared with older Arendsii types. Bred for improved tolerance of heavier shade and greater heat and drought resistance than typical astilbe, it holds up well in warm-summer gardens as long as soil moisture is maintained. Spent plumes dry to a rich caramel tone and can be left standing for winter texture; divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep the display vigorous.

common_name: Color Flash Lime Astilbe (Chartreuse-Foliage False Spirea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in evenly moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in light shade or filtered sun; a sport of Color Flash grown chiefly for its brilliant chartreuse-to-lime spring foliage rather than its flowers.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade or filtered sun, where the foliage color develops best. Color Flash Lime emerges in spring with vivid chartreuse-to-lime leaves edged in red, gradually shifting to burgundy-purple through summer and finishing gold in fall, so the plant earns its keep well before the soft pale-pink flower plumes rise above the foliage in early summer. Because the foliage display is the main event, siting it where morning sun reaches the leaves without scorching them intensifies the color contrast. Keep soil consistently moist through summer heat and mulch to protect the shallow crown; divide clumps every three to four years in spring once flowering or foliage vigor declines.

common_name: Rock and Roll Astilbe (White-Plumed Bronze-Foliage False Spirea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Rock and Roll is prized for its heavy production of pure white plumes against dark, bronze-tinted foliage.

directions: Set crowns just below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Rock and Roll forms a mound of dark, bronze-green, finely cut foliage on reddish stems, from which long, shimmering white plumes rise in mid- to late summer in far greater quantity than older white astilbe cultivars, making it a strong choice for brightening a dim corner of the garden. The dense flower spikes hold up well as cut flowers and dry attractively in place if left standing through fall. Keep the shallow root zone evenly moist and mulched, since astilbe foliage scorches quickly in dry soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to sustain heavy bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted plantlets in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; foliage color is brightest with a bit of filtered morning light, while deeper shade shifts the leaves toward chartreuse-green.

directions: A sport of the variegated cultivar 'Eco-Butterfly', 'Harvest Moon' replaces the usual silver-veined green foliage of strawberry begonia with rounded, fuzzy leaves in sulfur-yellow to gold, often flushed burgundy on the reverse and along the margins. Like the species, it spreads by thin red runners that root at the tip to form new plantlets, quickly knitting into a low, glowing mat under trees or along a shaded path edge. In late spring, wiry stems lift airy sprays of small white flowers with pink-spotted throats above the foliage, though the plant is grown chiefly for its color rather than bloom. Keep soil consistently moist and provide shelter from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the thin, colorful leaves.
